newsitem.title: GERMANY: ProSieben shares buoyant in grey market before IPO.
newsitem.headline: ProSieben shares buoyant in grey market before IPO.

text.p: Shares in German television network Pro Sieben AG were buoyant and well above their initial public offering price on Monday in grey market dealings ahead of the start of share market dealings set for later in the day.
Pro Sieben shares were trading at 106.00 to 110.00 marks, according to share market dealers, after earlier trading as high as 112 marks in morning dealings.
But the shares were below the 120 marks seen last week.
"The dealings are very active," said one trader. "I think the bids will remain relatively strong."
One trader said he expected the cash market fixing price for Pro Sieben to be above 100 marks, which is above the offering price set on Saturday at 72 marks.
"It looks like we can be a little bit above 100 marks at the start," the trader said.
Pro Sieben, whose offering was 50 times oversubscribed, is set to become the first German television broadcaster to list its shares on the stock market.
The network said only one in 10 bidders will receive any shares at all, and even winners will get only a portion of the shares they ordered.
The issue price was at the top of the range announced last week at the end of the 10-day book-building period.
The issue will raise 1.26 billion marks ($720 million) for the company, and increase its capital by 360 million marks to over 700 million marks.
The issue is being managed by a banking consortium led by BHF-Bank AG, Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG, and Salomon Brothers.

A total 850 million shares were ordered though only 17.5 million will go on the market. The network said 52.5 percent of the issue will be placed with German individual investors. Thirty-three percent of the orders came from outside Germany.
Due to the high degree of oversubscription, the company said a complex lottery would be used to fill the orders.

The company is also restructuring its shareholder structure to make Thomas Kirch, son of Bavarian media mogul Leo Kirch, its majority shareholder with 60 percent of the ordinary voting shares. Retail group Rewe holds the remaining 40 percent.
